one_liner: SQLite fork with a prolly-tree storage engine that adds Git-style branch, merge and diff; 1.1-2.9x slower than SQLite, not faster.
what_it_does: DoltLite keeps SQLite's parser, planner, VDBE and sqlite3_* C API but replaces everything below the btree.h seam with a content-addressed prolly tree in a single chunk-store file. Version control is exposed as SQL functions and virtual tables (dolt_commit, dolt_branch, dolt_merge, dolt_diff_<table>, dolt_history_<table>, push/pull/clone to remotes), and each connection can sit on its own branch. Existing code links libdoltlite instead of libsqlite3 and keeps its SQL, but the on-disk format is not SQLite's.
how_it_is_fast: It is not a speed play: the prolly tree (content-addressed immutable nodes with rolling-hash chunk boundaries, as in Dolt) exists to make diff, merge and structural sharing across history cheap, and it costs time on ordinary SQL. What keeps the gap to SQLite at 1.1-1.6x for wrapped workloads is a 64 MiB chunk/node cache (cache_size), an append-only chunk WAL with periodic checkpoints instead of a page journal, and the unchanged SQLite front end; every chunk read from the file is verified against its BLAKE3 address. Durable per-statement commits remain about 3x SQLite's WAL path.
when_to_use: You want an embedded SQL database with branches, commits, three-way merge, row-level diff and history queries (dolt_diff_<table>, dolt_history_<table>, dolt_blame_<table>) for local-first or agent workflows, and can accept SQLite-class but slower throughput.
Syncing a database between devices or with Dolt-style remotes (push, pull, clone, lazy clones) where shipping only changed chunks matters more than raw query latency.
Workloads that batch writes into explicit transactions and keep the working set inside the cache budget: there the report shows 1.0-1.3x SQLite for file-backed reads and writes.

Applications already written against the sqlite3_* API or a SQLite binding (Python, Go, Rust, Node, .NET, Swift, Android and WASM packages exist) that need versioning without moving to a server database.
when_not_to_use: When you want something faster than SQLite: every aggregate in the nightly report is slower (in-memory reads 1.2x, in-memory writes 1.6x, file-backed reads and writes 1.1x, durable autocommit writes 2.9x), and the release notes for v0.50.11-v0.50.15 show the same 1.0-3.7x range.
Commit-heavy OLTP with one statement per transaction: autocommit writes run 2.5-3.2x slower than SQLite in WAL mode with synchronous=FULL, and the nightly gate tolerates up to 5.5x.

Working sets larger than the chunk cache: the pragma docs say chunks are re-read and BLAKE3-verified on every pass once the budget is exceeded, and the 100,000-row nightly fixtures never exercise that regime.

Software that relies on SQLite file-format or pager semantics: no rollback journal or WAL files, journal_mode/page_size/mmap_size pragmas are inert, multi-database atomic commits are refused, non-integer primary keys become clustered NOT NULL keys, and the file cannot be read by stock SQLite.

Production systems that cannot tolerate beta-quality merge logic: the project is labelled Beta and on 2026-10-06 alone filed P1 issues such as a merge committing duplicate keys (#3695) and conflict resolution leaving a row an index lookup cannot find (#3691).

integration.form: static lib (libdoltlite.a) or shared lib (libdoltlite.so/.dylib), plus CLI and language bindings
integration.dependencies: zlib, pthreads, libm (link -lpthread -lz -lm); Tcl for building from source on MSYS2; vec1 vector extension built in by default
integration.min_toolchain: C compiler with autoconf-style ./configure && make (SQLite 3.54.0 code base); compiler version requirements not documented
integration.platforms: Linux x86_64 and arm64, macOS Apple Silicon (prebuilt), Windows via MSYS2/MinGW64 and prebuilt x64 tools, WebAssembly (ext/wasm)
integration.thread_safety: SQLite threading modes apply; across connections and processes one durable writer at a time via a graph-lock sidecar (concurrent writers get SQLITE_BUSY), readers stay live during writes and GC
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same sqlite3_* API, symbol names and SQL semantics, and stock SQLite files still open on the original B-tree engine, but DoltLite-format files are a different on-disk format and storage-coupled pragmas and behaviours differ

gotchas: The per-row 'wins' in the report are harness artifacts: in file_reads and file_writes stock SQLite runs in default rollback-journal mode (only PRAGMA cache_size=16384 is added) and every read statement is its own transaction; with the same SQL in WAL mode (ac_reads) SQLite's oltp_point_select drops from 64.75 ms to 30.19 ms and DoltLite ties or loses on every row, about 3.5 us of rollback-mode overhead per statement (derived from page data). The 0.7-0.9x file_writes rows are also against the rollback journal, and no WAL-mode wrapped-write run exists to check them.

The timer (test/sysbench_timer.c) runs each workload as one sqlite3_exec script, so every statement is parsed and prepared afresh in both engines; that shared front-end cost sits in both sides of each ratio, so the storage-layer slowdown is larger than the 1.1-1.6x headline ratios suggest.

The 'stock SQLite' baseline is the fork's own SQLite 3.54.0 tree built with DOLTLITE_PROLLY=0 on a shared ubuntu-latest runner with configure-default flags and no CPU model; test/build_stock_reference.sh records that CI once shipped a reference that silently used DoltLite storage and passed by construction, so older reports and blog numbers may be invalid.

Open time grows with the chunk WAL since the last checkpoint (thresholds DOLTLITE_WAL_CHECKPOINT_THRESHOLD and DOLTLITE_WAL_CHECKPOINT_CHUNKS), space is reclaimed only by dolt_gc/VACUUM, and PRAGMA page_size echoes whatever you set even though no pages exist.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over the SQLite-beating siblings (CalicoDB, mpedb, ForestDB, BTreePlus) only when you need versioned SQL with branch/merge/diff semantics, since they are faster key-value or B-tree engines without history; for raw embedded speed LMDB or stock SQLite remain the better choice.
verified_claims_summary: The project's nightly report (2026-10-06, commit 3e4ff81, GitHub-hosted ubuntu24 runner, cc -O2 harness, 100,000-row sysbench-style fixtures, medians of 55 paired alternating runs) shows DoltLite slower than a stock SQLite reference built from the same tree on every aggregate: 1.2x in-memory reads, 1.6x in-memory writes, 1.1x file-backed reads and writes and 2.9x durable autocommit writes; the handful of file-backed rows where DoltLite is faster exist only against rollback-journal SQLite and vanish against SQLite in WAL mode.
status_note: Very active beta (commits daily through 2026-10-07, releases weekly, v0.50.15 on 2026-10-05, format version 12 frozen) under Apache-2.0 for DoltLite code with public-domain SQLite sources; usable as a library today, but merge and schema-merge correctness bugs are still being filed and fixed at a high rate.
